standards: Explain, using two invented near-miss stories, how a poor handover leads to a missed task, and name the cause in each story.
Summarize a patient's status aloud from a case card in Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation order, in about 60 seconds with no missing items.
Clarify an unclear instruction in a role-play by asking one repeat-back question and asking the listener to repeat the plan back to confirm the meaning.
Select plain words instead of slang or unapproved abbreviations from a list of phrases, getting at least 18 of 20 correct.
Demonstrate a handover under two minutes in a live role-play, using the agreed order and confirming who holds each open task.
Show you can hand over from a new case card in the agreed order and reflect on one thing to improve, meeting the role-play checklist.
Describe what makes a care note clear, fair and useful, and give two reasons why a note must be accurate for the next reader.
Record an event from a short scenario with date, time, facts only and signature, meeting every item on the checklist.
Correct an error in a sample note with one line, the word error, initials and date, keeping the original readable, and mark a late entry.
Protect privacy by removing every personal detail not needed for care from a sample note, and say who may read a note.
Write a note for a short scenario about a fall with no injury, then score it against the checklist and name any gaps.
Distinguish fact from opinion in 10 sample lines, getting at least 9 correct, and reflect on one way to improve your own notes.
Introduce yourself and your role in a role-play with the agreed greeting, using the patient's name correctly and respectfully.
Explain a care step from a care card in plain words so the listener can repeat it back correctly.
Respond to a worried family member with Listen, Acknowledge, Explain and Check, using calm, respectful words and making no promises you cannot keep.
Decide when an interpreter is needed and describe how to use an approved service, without relying on a family member or child to translate.
Escalate a concern with a short message stating who, what and when, in writing and by voice, following the local route.
Demonstrate the four steps in a live role-play, using teach-back at least twice to confirm the person understood.
Show you can handle a new case card, including a request for information you may not share, and reflect on two things to improve.
Explain what a home visit is for and where its limits lie, and state what to do when the person refuses help.
Identify risk signs in a case summary, such as unsafe cooking, trip hazards or neglect, and list at least six factors with the source of each.
Rate a visit as Low, Medium or High using the three-level scale, and state the action each rating needs, including same-day manager contact for High.
Talk with the person respectfully in a role-play, starting from their own view of their situation and listening before you advise.
Record a visit note with facts seen, rating, action, who was told and the time, written promptly on the same day.
Apply the scale to a case card such as Person F or Person M by listing signs, giving a rating and naming the first action.
Show you can plan, rate and record a visit from a new case summary and report a concern to a supervisor in the agreed time.
Decide whether a situation counts as a concern, using a short scenario, and give the reason for your decision.
Write a concern report with the exact words in quotes, date, time and witness, using facts only and no opinion.
Select the correct reporting route from your organisation's policy and tell the right person within the required time, including the alternative route.
Protect confidentiality by sharing only what the route needs, and explain to the person who must be told instead of promising secrecy.
Write and score a report for a case card, such as an unexplained burn or a bruise, and choose who to tell from the route card.
Reflect on one sample record and name two things to improve, using the fact-not-opinion test.
Explain what person-centred means and show how the person's own goals, strengths and wishes lead a review.
Prepare a review from a case file, listing the person's goals, strengths and questions first, and invite everyone with a clear agenda and a welcoming setting.
Facilitate a short review in a role-play so the person speaks first, last and for at least half the time, redirecting anyone who talks over them.
Write an action plan from meeting notes in which every action has a named owner and a date, and set the next review date.
Record the outcome in plain language in the person's own words on the review form and care plan, and share it with the person.
Plan and run a review for a case card, such as Person H or Person N, and write three actions with owners and dates.
Evaluate a review against a checklist, scoring each item with one reason, and name one change for next time.
Write three lesson outcomes for a given topic, each starting with a measurable Bloom action verb, and replace vague verbs such as know or understand.
Match each activity and each check to one outcome in a plan, and spot an activity that does not lead to its outcome.
Design a five-item check for one outcome that a learner can pass or not yet pass, with one correct answer per item.
Plan the timing and flow of a lesson so that each activity fits the time available and leads on to the next.
Draft a lesson of your own with two to four outcomes, one aligned activity for each, and a check for each outcome.
Review a peer's plan against a checklist, giving two strengths and one improvement, and show your own lesson meets the outcome standard.
Explain why short checks during a lesson tell you what to do next, and describe how often to use them.
Select a check type, such as an exit slip, mini whiteboards or a hands-up poll, that matches the verb in the lesson goal.
Interpret a class result table quickly, naming the two weakest topics, and share class patterns rather than individual marks.
Plan a short re-teach for the weakest topic with one new example, and set a re-check of a few items within a week.
Construct five clear questions for a topic, each with one correct answer and no trick wording.
Interpret a new result table, rank the weakest aims, plan the next step, and record the pattern on a simple class tracker.
Show that the outcome stays the same while the route changes, by writing three levels of one task that all lead to that outcome.
Identify learner needs from a class profile and choose a scaffold for each, such as prompts, a word bank or pictures.
Modify a task with an extension for fast learners, such as an open question or asking them to create a problem, without raising the standard for others.
Adjust time and the room for a learner who needs it, such as extra time or seating, while keeping the standard unchanged.
Adapt a ten-item worksheet into three levels and write a five-line note explaining each change and the learner need behind it.
Evaluate your adapted lesson against a checklist, giving two changes for next time and one reason for each grouping.
